mappings.note: The answer is that droughts, floods and cyclones are becoming more frequent, so forecasts matter for preparedness - squarely the disaster outcome. Not C-SST1.1, because the craft of forecasting is assumed and the stake is safety.
Asks for a worked example of a warning saving lives - evacuating a coast, keeping fishermen ashore. Preventive action in the event of a disaster, not the LO-5 lane of ordinary daily adaptation.

Reads the IMD yellow level as 'watch, stay updated' - interpreting a hazard warning. Not LO-4, which is used for the map-legend items where the task is reading symbols rather than acting on a risk level.
Names weather conditions from the icons in a map legend, so the skill is map reading. Not LO-6, because the item only harvests symbols and never asks what to do about them.
Separates weather as the momentary state of the atmosphere from climate as the long-run average. Not LO-4, because climate is only defined here, not located as regions.

Argues why 'time' and 'place' belong in the definition of weather - the atmosphere's state being local and changeable. Not LO-4: coastal versus inland is an illustration of variability, not a region to be located.
Coconut oil solidifying and curd setting slowly in cold weather is temperature acting on everyday household life. Not LO-3, because the atmosphere is not what is explained - the kitchen effect is.

Traces the full water cycle - solar heating, evaporation, condensation, precipitation - behind the IMD motto. The fullest of the three motto items and the clearest atmospheric-process answer among them.

The comparison is of what people endure at sea level and at Khardung La - breathlessness, fatigue, acclimatisation (LO-5) - resting on thinner air and lower pressure with height (LO-3). Neither half alone covers the expected answer.
Wind data as it bears on pilots, sailors and farmers is weather shaping working life. Not C-SST1.1, because the instruments are not the subject; the professions' decisions are.
Explains evaporation, its cooling effect and how ambient humidity speeds or slows it - an atmospheric-moisture mechanism. Drying clothes is the illustration, so LO-5 would misplace the emphasis.

Values an AWS both as observation technology that removes people from a dangerous site (C-SST1.1) and as the source of early warnings for glacial-lake floods (LO-6). The Sikkim item earlier was pure LO-6 because it asked only where the station is and why.
Evaluates forecasting inside disaster management - evacuation, health advisories, resource mobilisation. The most direct LO-6 item in the chapter; C-SST1.1 would reduce it to a question about method.
Defends traditional nature-reading as a hyperlocal complement to scientific forecasting - a judgement about ways of observing. Not LO-6, because no specific hazard or response is in view.
Wind as air flowing from high to low pressure as the atmosphere seeks balance - the mechanism inside the atmosphere. Not C-SST1.1, because no anemometer or measurement appears.

Wind direction and speed are argued through their consequences - where rain or pollution travels, seed dispersal, soil erosion, danger to flights. That impact-on-people framing is LO-5, whereas the parallel item on how an anemometer works stayed with C-SST1.1.
Argues that precise instruments replaced subjective observation and made models possible - the development of measurement itself. Not LO-3, because no atmospheric property is explained.
Clothing, plans and comfort adjusted to forecasts is the everyday adaptation outcome. Not LO-6, because nothing hazardous is involved - these are ordinary daily choices.

A farmer timing a pesticide spray around the Loo and 42C heat is a working decision driven by weather. Not LO-6: strong afternoon wind here is a nuisance to plan around, not a disaster to prepare for.

Part (iii) asks what safety precaution the climbers should take on a deteriorating forecast (LO-6), while parts (i) and (ii) rest on reading a 15 mb fall as an approaching depression (LO-3). The pressure reasoning is load-bearing, so both are cited.

Part (iii), why humidity must be controlled to save paintings, is weather governing human work (LO-5); part (ii) asks explicitly which instrument measures it (C-SST1.1). Not LO-7, because mould is a moisture problem, not pollution.

Parts (i) and (ii) are about the rain gauge and what a 150 mm reading means (C-SST1.1); part (iii) draws out how sharply rainfall varies between Cherrapunji and Shillong, which is spatial distribution (LO-4).

Pressure for altimetry and wind for the flight are weather governing an occupation (LO-5), while part (ii) turns on dry Jaipur against humid Kochi, a contrast between places (LO-4). Not C-SST1.1, since no instrument is named in the question.
